n: Now secure as king, David turns to a spiritual goal: bringing the ark of the covenant to his new capital. He gathers a huge honor guard of chosen men.

The ark had sat neglected for about two decades at Baale (Kirjath-jearim). It was Israel’s most sacred object, the symbol of God’s presence, called by His name and pictured as His throne between the cherubim.

f.g: Another name for Kirjath-jearim, about nine miles west of Jerusalem.
The two golden cherubim on the ark’s lid (the mercy seat) were seen as the footstool or throne of the invisible God.

n: They put the ark on a brand-new ox cart. It looked honorable, but the law said the ark must be carried on poles on the shoulders of Levites. The Philistines had once moved it by cart, and Israel copies them.

f.g: Here simply “the hill” — the hill in Kirjath-jearim where Abinadab lived.

n: Abinadab’s son Ahio walks in front of the ark, guiding the oxen, while his brother Uzzah walks beside it.
A grand procession follows, with joyful music on every kind of instrument. Their intentions are good and their worship is sincere.

f.g: Chronicles reads “with all their might and with singing” (1 Chronicles 13:8); the Hebrew words are similar.
Psalteries = stringed instruments like lyres or harps; timbrels = hand drums or tambourines.

n: At a threshing floor the oxen stumble, and Uzzah reaches out to steady the ark.

f.g: A flat, hard open area where grain was beaten to separate it from the husks.

n: God strikes Uzzah dead. It seems severe to modern readers, but the law warned that even Levites must not touch the holy things. The lesson: sacred things must be handled in God’s way, not merely with good intentions.

f.w: God smote him there for his error

f.g: The Hebrew word is uncertain; it may mean rashness or irreverence.

n: David is upset and names the place “the breaking out against Uzzah.” The joyful event has turned to tragedy.

f.g: “The breach (or outburst) against Uzzah.” Compare Baal-perazim in 2 Samuel 5:20.

n: David is afraid. He realizes that God’s holy presence is not something to take lightly, and wonders whether he can bring the ark near at all.

f.w: How shall the ark of the LORD come to me?

n: So he leaves it at the house of Obed-edom, a man from Gath — perhaps a Philistine follower of David, or a Levite from the town of Gath-rimmon.

f.g: Gittite = from Gath. A Levite named Obed-edom later serves the ark (1 Chronicles 15:18, 24).

n: For three months the ark stays there, and the Lord blesses Obed-edom’s whole household. God’s presence, treated with reverence, brings blessing rather than judgment.
Encouraged by the blessings on Obed-edom’s house, David tries again, this time with great joy. Chronicles adds that now the Levites carried the ark properly.
After the bearers take just six steps — and nothing goes wrong — David offers sacrifices, thanking God and seeking His acceptance.
David dances with all his strength in pure joy before the Lord. He wears a simple linen ephod, a priestly-style garment, instead of his royal robes.

f.w: danced before the LORD with all his might

f.g: A short linen garment worn by priests and those serving in worship.

n: The whole nation joins in with shouts and trumpet blasts, bringing the ark up to Jerusalem.
Michal, Saul’s daughter, watches from a window and despises David in her heart. Note that she is called “Saul’s daughter” here, not David’s wife — the narrator hints at where her loyalties lie.
The ark is placed in a tent David had set up for it. He offers burnt offerings (fully devoted to God) and peace offerings (shared in a fellowship meal).
Like a father of the nation, David blesses the people in the Lord’s name.
David gives every person, women and men alike, a gift of food to celebrate. The whole nation shares in the joy.

f.g: The Hebrew probably means a cake of raisins or dates rather than a jug of wine.

n: Michal meets David with biting sarcasm, accusing him of shamelessly exposing himself before servant girls, acting undignified for a king.

f.g: Without his royal robe, the short ephod may have exposed more than was considered proper for a king.

n: David replies that he was worshipping the Lord, who chose him over Saul’s family. His joy was directed to God, not to impressing people.

f.w: which chose me before thy father

n: David says he will humble himself even more before God, and the humble servant girls will honor him for it. True greatness comes through humility before the Lord.

f.w: of them shall I be had in honour

n: Michal remains childless all her life. Whatever the cause, this means no descendant of Saul would sit on David’s throne.

f.g: Childlessness was a deep sorrow in Israel; here it also marks the end of Saul’s hopes through Michal.
